source_text: Otiosum est ire per singulos et totam seriem generis istius explicare, quum in primis parentibus probata mortalitas in caeteros ipso ordine successionis influxerit: nisi forte post mortem deos fingitis, et, pejerante Proculo, deus Romulus, et Juba, Mauris volentibus, deus est, et divi caeteri reges, qui consecrantur, non ad fidem numinis, sed ad honorem emeritae potestatis. Invitis his denique hoc nomen adscribitur: optant in homine perseverare; fieri se deos metuunt, etsi jam senes, nolunt. Ergo nec de mortuis dii sunt, quoniam Deus mori non posset ; nec de natis, quoniam moritur omne quod nascitur, divinum autem id est quod nec ortum habet nec occasum. Cur enim, si nati sunt, non hodieque nascuntur? nisi forte jam Jupiter senuit et partus in Junone defecit, et Minerva canuit antequam peperit. An ideo cessavit ista generatio, quoniam nulla hujusmodi fabulis praebetur adsensio? Caeterum, si dii creare possent, interire non possent; plures totis hominibus deos haberemus, ut jam eos nec coelum contineret, nec aer caperet, nec terra gestaret: unde manifestum est homines illos fuisse quos et natos legimus et mortuos scimus. Quis ergo dubitat horum imagines consecratas vulgus orare et publice colere? dum opinio et mens imperitorum artis concinnitate decipitur, auri fulgore praestringitur, argenti nitore et candore eboris hebetatur. Quod si in animum quis inducat tormentis quibus et quibus machinis simulacrum omne formetur, erubescet timere se materiem ab artifice, ut deum faceret, illusam. Deus enim ligneus, rogi fortasse vel infelicis stipitis portio, suspenditur, caeditur, dolatur, runcinatur; et deus aureus, vel argenteus, de immundo vasculo saepius, ut factum Aegyptio regi, conflatur, tunditur malleis et incudibus figuratur; et lapideus caeditur, scalpitur et ab impurato homine laevigatur; nec sentit suae nativitatis injuriam, ita ut nec postea de vestra veneratione culturam: nisi forte nondum deus saxum est, vel lignum, vel argentum. Quando igitur hic nascitur? ecce funditur, fabricatur, sculpitur; nondum deus est: ecce plumbatur, construitur, erigitur; nec adhuc deus est: ecce ornatur, consecratur, oratur: tunc postremo deus est quum homo illum voluit et dedicavit.
pass_a_gloss: It is idle to go through each one and to explain the whole series of this kind, since in the first parents mortality has been proven and has flowed into the others by the very order of succession: unless perhaps after death you imagine gods, and, with Proculus perjuring, Romulus is a god, and Juba, with the Moors willing, is a god, and the other divine kings, who are consecrated, not to the faith of divinity, but to the honor of deserved power. Finally, this name is ascribed to these men against their will: they wish to persevere in man; they fear to become gods, even if they are already old, they do not want to. Therefore, neither are the dead gods, since God cannot die; nor are the born gods, since everything that is born dies, but the divine is that which has neither origin nor decay. Why, if they were born, do they not still give birth today? unless perhaps Jupiter has already grown old and childbirth has failed in Juno, and Minerva has turned gray before giving birth. Or has this generation ceased because no assent is given to such fables? Moreover, if gods could create, they could not perish; we would have more gods than all men, so that neither heaven nor air nor earth could contain them: from which it is clear that those were men whom we read were born and whom we know died. Who then doubts that the consecrated images of these men are worshiped and publicly honored by the crowd? while the opinion and mind of the unskilled are deceived by the harmony of art, dazzled by the splendor of gold, and dulled by the shine of silver and the whiteness of ivory. But if someone brings into their mind the torments by which and the machines by which every image is formed, they will blush to fear the material deceived by the artisan, so that it makes a god. For a wooden god, perhaps a portion of a funeral pyre or a unlucky tree, is hung, cut, carved, and polished; and a golden god, or a silver one, is often melted from an unclean vessel, as was made for the Egyptian king, and is shaped by hammers and anvils; and a stone god is cut, carved, and polished by an impure man; and it does not feel the injury of its birth, so that it does not feel the cultivation of your veneration afterwards: unless perhaps the stone, or the wood, or the silver is not yet a god. When then is this god born? behold, it is melted, fabricated, carved; it is not yet a god: behold, it is soldered, constructed, erected; it is not yet a god: behold, it is ornamented, consecrated, worshiped: then finally it is a god when a man has willed and dedicated it.

pass_b_english: There is no point in running through each name and laying out the whole line of such figures, because mortality was proved in the very first ancestors and then passed down to all the rest by the sheer logic of succession — unless you insist on inventing gods after death. Proculus perjures himself and Romulus becomes a god; the Moors consent and Juba becomes a god; other kings are consecrated not as a testimony to divinity but as an honor to the power they earned. In the end the title is forced on these men against their will: they want to stay human; they dread becoming gods, and even in old age they refuse it. Therefore the dead cannot be gods, since God cannot die; and the born cannot be gods, since everything born must die, whereas the divine is what has neither beginning nor end. If they were born once, why are they not still being born today? Unless Jupiter has grown old and Juno has lost the power of childbirth, and Minerva turned gray before she ever gave birth. Or did that whole generation stop simply because no one any longer believes such fables? Besides, if gods could create they could not perish; we would have more gods than all humanity, so that heaven could not hold them, the air could not contain them, and the earth could not bear them. That makes it clear: those we read were born and know died were simply men. Who then doubts that the crowd worships and publicly venerates the consecrated images of those men? The opinions and minds of the unskilled are deceived by the harmony of the craft, blinded by the flash of gold, dulled by the gleam of silver and the whiteness of ivory. But if anyone brings to mind the torments and the machines by which every image is shaped, he will blush to fear a material that the artisan has tricked into passing for a god. A wooden god — perhaps a piece of a funeral pyre or an unlucky tree — is hung, cut, carved, and planed; a golden or silver god is often melted from a filthy vessel, as was done for the Egyptian king, and hammered and forged on anvils; a stone god is cut, carved, and polished by an impure man. It feels none of the injury of its own making, so it cannot afterward feel the cultivation of your veneration — unless the stone, the wood, or the silver is not yet a god. So when is this god born? Watch: it is melted, fabricated, carved — not yet a god. Watch: it is soldered, assembled, erected — still not a god. Watch: it is adorned, consecrated, prayed to — only then does it finally become a god, because a man willed it and dedicated it.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal gloss, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that preserves all nuances, including the conditional clauses, the specific list of materials/actions, and the theological distinctions regarding mortality and divinity. All clauses in the Latin source are accounted for in both English versions.
